assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made the single-photon, single-artificial-atom regime controllable on a chip: strong coupling, dispersive readout, and the architecture underlying transmon-based processors and microwave quantum optics. It is a clean case of a basic quantum phenomenon becoming an enabling platform, and it has been reproduced and extended in many laboratories. Close to my own field, so I note that bias.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) split credit between theory and experiment. Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff give a theory-plus-two-experiment configuration; Girvin has a strong claim and the cap of three forces an uncomfortable choice.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: two decades of independent confirmation across many groups, with the interpretation stable. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes timing sensitive, since the committee may judge the neighbouring area recently rewarded, but this is a distinct discovery.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits may argue for waiting.
Allocation of credit between Girvin, Blais and the experimental leaders is unresolved.
My professional closeness to this community may bias my assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals (trapped-ion quantum gates, 1995, and cold-atom quantum simulation with Hubbard physics) provided the theoretical blueprint for two experimental platforms that are now central to quantum information. The originality and lasting impact are high and the physics is clearly formulated.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the natural, tightly linked pair; the credited list contains only these two, which gives a clean two-person prize. Experimental realisation by others (Wineland, Blatt and others) is not in this candidate.
assessment.maturity: Mature: trapped-ion gates and atomic quantum simulators are demonstrated by many groups. Recognition of theory is timely given experimental maturity, though a prize for theory alone has to fit with the experimental prizes already given (Haroche, Wineland 2012).
uncertainties: A theory-only prize may be seen as incomplete without the experimental groups.
Overlap with the Hubbard quantum simulation candidate may split support.
I am relying on my own recollection of the original 1995 and 1998 papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84, E91) turned the foundations of quantum mechanics into a concrete information-theoretic protocol and launched quantum communication. Originality and conceptual clarity are outstanding, and the work links entanglement and Bell inequalities to practical cryptography.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard for BB84 and Ekert for the entanglement-based protocol is the natural trio; Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a historical complication, and Wiesner is not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle with commercial and satellite demonstrations, though practical security against device imperfections remains an active topic. Recognition after more than 35 years is not premature; the 2022 prize for entanglement experiments partly covered the neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Wiesner's earlier contribution is outside the credited names.
Practical security is not fully settled and the discovery-versus-application distinction needs care.
The 2022 prize for Bell tests overlaps in scope.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Loss-DiVincenzo proposal for spin qubits in quantum dots and the subsequent experimental demonstration of coherent single-spin control and two-qubit gates opened a leading semiconductor route to quantum computing, with compatibility with silicon manufacturing. The physics of how spin and charge are controlled is rich and carefully verified.
assessment.attribution: Loss and DiVincenzo for the theoretical proposal and Vandersypen for the experimental realisation form a reasonable theory-plus-experiment prize; other experimental leaders (for instance Kouwenhoven, Marcus, Morello, Dzurak) have strong claims that cannot all fit within three names.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: single and two-qubit gates have exceeded error-correction thresholds in silicon in several groups, but scaling is still ahead. Somewhat early compared with superconducting qubits.
uncertainties: Experimental credit is spread across several groups, so the exclusion of some is a real risk.
Scalability remains unproven and may make recognition premature.
I defer somewhat to colleagues on semiconductor materials details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade gives strong, switchable atom-atom interactions that enable programmable neutral-atom arrays for quantum simulation and quantum computing, and the arrays have rapidly become a leading platform with demonstrations of many-body phases and logical-qubit operations. The physics is clear and new regimes of controllable interaction have been opened.
assessment.attribution: The original blockade proposal (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller, Lukin and others, 2000) and the early blockade experiments (Grangier, Browaeys, Saffman) mean credit is spread; Browaeys, Saffman and Lukin is one workable configuration, with Grangier an equally defensible alternative. Lukin appears under several candidates, which matters for the overall allocation.
assessment.maturity: Intermediate: strong independent confirmation from several groups, but the field is moving fast and the interpretation of the best-performing architecture is still being worked out. Probably slightly early.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among the original proposers, early experimenters and array developers is unresolved.
Rapid evolution suggests that the prize-worthy core may still be shifting.
Lukin spans several candidates, which could complicate configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and are enabling tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The importance of controlled quantum systems for precision measurement is evident, and the discovery is clean and measurable.
assessment.attribution: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations and refinement make a compelling pair; others (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg) contributed but the supplied credit gives a clear two-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent groups reproduce and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, and international clock comparisons are routine. The redefinition of the second would strengthen the case for timing, but this is not a requirement. Hall and Hänsch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes in precision metrology might reduce enthusiasm.
Ye also appears under the ultracold molecules candidate.
Contributions of other clock pioneers outside the list are not credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation answered the fundamental question of whether fragile quantum information can be protected, and they define the roadmap for scalable quantum computers. I personally believe that full-scale error correction is what will make quantum processors useful, so the conceptual importance is very high.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane for the first codes and Kitaev for topological and fault-tolerant ideas is a reasonable trio, but Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or and others are not in the credited list and the contribution is broad, so a fair attribution is hard.
assessment.maturity: Experimental error correction below threshold has recently been shown in superconducting circuits and neutral atoms, but fault-tolerant machines are still ahead; the discovery is theoretical and the physical relevance is only now being confirmed. Probably premature for a prize as of 2026.
uncertainties: Large and diffuse authorship makes a three-person prize hard to defend.
Practical, scalable fault tolerance is still not demonstrated, so recognition may be premature.
Whether this counts as physics rather than computer science is open for some colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and demonstrating quantum control and entanglement with macroscopic objects extend quantum physics to massive systems and underpin quantum transduction and sensing. The link to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects is thematically notable, and I know the superconducting-circuit side of this work well.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (quantum ground state and phonon quantum control in a circuit-coupled resonator), Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg (cavity optomechanics, sideband cooling) cover different routes; other groups (Teufel, Lehnert, Painter, Schwab) have equally strong claims, so allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, with independent demonstrations in multiple platforms since 2010, but the application horizon is less clear and tests of fundamental questions about macroscopic superposition are not yet complete.
uncertainties: Many comparably strong groups are excluded by the three-name limit.
The foundational payoff, such as tests of gravity-related decoherence, is not yet shown.
Thematic proximity to the 2025 prize could weigh against it.
